title: Leingang v. Pierce County Medical Bureau, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Dennis Leingang filed suit against his health insurance provider, the Pierce County Medical Bureau, seeking unpaid benefits and alleging that it had violated Washington's Consumer Protection Act (§19.86.020) by engaging in unfair and deceptive practices after it had invoked an exclusion clause in Leingang's insurance contract to deny him reimbursement for medical expenses incurred in an automobile accident that were covered by his automobile insurance. The trial court dismissed Leingang's claim, ruling that the exclusion was enforceable and not contrary to public policy. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision after the Supreme Court of Washington had in the interim held that exclusions of the sort invoked by the Pierce County Medical Bureau violate public policy, ordering the contested benefits to be paid to Leingang and remanding the case to the trial court to resolve the Consumer Protection Act claim. The Pierce County Medical Bureau appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Pierce County Medical Bureau engage in an unfair and deceptive practice by denying benefits pursuant to a clause subsequently declared to be in violation of public policy?
conclusions: Justice Guy's opinion for the Court held that the Pierce County Medical Bureau had not engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by invoking the exclusion clause in Leingang's policy as it had relied upon a reasonable interpretation of existing law in doing so. Although the Pierce County Medical Bureau had not requested a legal opinion from the Insurance Commissioner to determine whether its interpretation of the law was in fact reasonable, it was not legally required to do so by any statute or regulation.

title: Ino Ino, Inc. v. Bellevue
facts: Respondent Ino Ino, Inc. filed suit in the Superior Court for King County to challenge the constitutionality of the city of Bellevue's ordinance regulating adult cabarets. The ordinance regulated various aspects of the operations of adult cabarets, prohibiting physical contact between dancers and customers, prohibiting nude performances or graphic representations thereof outside of adult cabarets, and imposing a licensing requirement for the managers of adult cabarets that entailed a 14-day processing period. The trial court upheld the constitutionality of the ordinance. Ino Ino appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the provisions of the ordinance stipulating that a minimum distance be maintained between dancers and customers in order to prevent physical contact constitute a reasonable time, place, or manner restriction upon expressive speech? Are the provisions of the ordinance prohibiting displays or graphic representations of nudity outside of adult cabarets unconstitutionally overbroad? Does the 14-day period required to process adult cabaret managers' applications represent an unconstitutional prior restraint upon speech?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the trial court's decision. The Court ruled that although the Washington State Constitution's guarantee of the right to freedom of speech (Article 1 §5) offers broader protection than the First Amendment to the United States Constitution to expressive speech, the prohibition of physical contact between dancers and customers was nonetheless constitutional as it promoted the important state interest in curbing the illegal secondary effects associated with adult cabarets without denying dancers the ability to convey their erotic message. However, the Court held that the ordinance's prohibition of displays and representations of nudity outside of adult cabarets was overbroad as the display of artistic works featuring nudity could fall within its scope. The Court also concluded that requiring that prospective managers of adult cabarets wait 14 days while their applications are processed imposed an unconstitutional prior restraint upon speech as the ordinance included no provision for the granting of temporary licenses.

title: Nelson v. McClatchy Newspapers, Inc.
facts: Washington's Fair Campaign Practices Act forbids employers from discriminating against employees on the basis of their political views and/or activities. Petitioner Sandra Nelson was employed as a reporter by The News Tribune, which objected to her public role as a local political activist on grounds that it undermined the newspaper's appearance of objectivity. Nelson's refusal to cease her political activities ultimately led to her reassignment, prompting her to file suit in the Superior Court for Pierce County on the basis of an alleged violation of the Fair Campaign Practices Act. The Superior Court granted summary judgment to respondent McClatchy Newspapers, Inc., ruling that The News Tribune's right to freedom of the press shielded it from liability. Nelson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Fair Campaign Practices Act bar employers from discriminating against employees for refusing to remain politically abstinent? If so, would applying the Fair Campaign Practices Act to The News Tribune violate the newspaper's right to freedom of the press under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §5 of the Washington State Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Sanders' opinion for the Court held that while the plain meaning of the Fair Campaign Practices Act encompassed discriminatory action by employers of the sort engaged in by The News Tribune, applying the statute to newspapers violates their 1st Amendment rights. In particular, the Court concluded that the broad protection given to press outlets' editorial discretion encompasses decisions made by newspapers such as The News Tribune that are intended to preserve their editorial integrity and credibility.

title: State of Washington v. Stephen B. Pick
questions: Did the trial court err in failing to grant a new trial when, before the verdict was read in open court, the prosecutor discussed with a juror inadmissible evidence regarding the defendant's prior conviction?

title: Michael H. Wallace, et ux., et al. v. Andrew Evans, et ux.
questions: Whether a motion to dismiss for want of prosecution may be granted where the case is noted for trial before the dismissal motion is heard, regardless of how long the plaintiff's action has been inactive.

title: State of Washington v. Darold Jay Stenson
questions: This is an appeal from a death sentence. The appellant's brief makes 33 assignments of error and states 41 issues. No attempt has been made to summarize those issues for this list.
